contributions.headingText: B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (B-ALL/LBL) with other defined genetic abnormalities includes neoplasms of lymphoblasts of B-cell lineage defined by the presence of specific newly described or uncommon genetic drivers.

2A70.Y Other B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma with recurrent genetic abnormalities

Acceptable: B-cell lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma NOS.

Not recommended: precursor B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma; B-cell acute lymphoid leukaemia; B-lymphoblastic lymphoma.

B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with DUX4 rearrangement; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with MEF2D rearrangement; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with ZNF384 rearrangement; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with PAX5alt; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with PAX5 p.P80R; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with NUTM1 rearrangement; B-lymphoblastic leukaemia with MYC rearrangement

B-ALL and B-LBL represent the same disease. B-ALL always involves the bone marrow and usually also involves the peripheral blood. Extramedullary involvement is common and is by definition the primary site of involvement in B-LBL. For details, see section B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma .
The presenting features are similar to those seen in other B-ALLs (see section B-lymphoblastic leukaemias/lymphomas: Introduction).
These represent approximately 10–15% of paediatric B-ALL/LBL cases and 20–35% of adult B-ALL/LBL cases {33895809; 34250504}; the individual subtypes are detailed in #30191Table 4.12 .

Like for other types, the initiating causes of these B-ALL/LBLs are unknown. For some B-ALL/LBL with other defined genetic alterations, a genetic predisposition is suggestive. Susceptibility to B-ALL/LBL has been described in patients with germline variants in the haematopoietic transcription factor gene PAX5 {24013638; 24287434; 33036026}.

The development of B-ALL/LBL, like other cancers, occurs secondary to cumulative disruptions of key cell regulatory pathways {21376230; 29395053; 32565969}. In particular, most dysregulations involve genes for self-renewal, cell proliferation, apoptosis, differentiation, or their signalling pathways {23612374; 25184049; 30697448; 31367767; 32247396}.

DUX4 activates the cleavage-specific transcriptional programme during embryogenesis, but it is normally repressed in adult tissue except for testis {28459457}. DUX4 rearrangement induces ectopic DUX4 expression in immature B cells and promotes leukaemogenesis in murine experimental models {27019113}. DUX4 overexpression results in loss of function of ERG, either by depletion or induced expression of a novel isoform, showing the interplay between DUX4 and ERG deregulation in leukaemogenesis in this subtype {27776115}.

MEF2D encodes a transcription factor expressed throughout B-cell differentiation and involved in early B-cell development {18800157; 26660426}. Chimeric proteins created by MEF2D fusion genes gain aberrant function mediated by the MEF2D transcriptional activation domain and confer haematopoietic self-renewal {27824051}. Mouse transplantation assays show that MEF2D fusion proteins have leukaemogenic activity in murine pro-B cells {27019113}. MEF2D fusion proteins alter the transcription of downstream genes, resulting in upregulation of pre-B-cell receptor components that contributes to B-cell proliferation and survival {34661138; 35544603}.

ZNF384 (CIZ) at 12p13.31 encodes a zinc finger transcription factor important for regulation of extracellular matrix genes {10669742}. ZNF384 rearrangements are understood to occur in a subset of haematopoietic stem cells {30209392; 31221673}. More than 10 ZNF384 translocation partners exist, including EP300, TCF3, CREBBP, SMARCA2, TAF15, and ARID1B {30643249; 30487223; 30630978; 33692463; 27392123}. These cryptic translocations that fuse the ZNF384 coding region in-frame to the partner gene forming the 3′ part of the fusion gene {34529760} can be observed in both B-ALL and B/myeloid mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia with the same transcriptional profile, and both leukaemias demonstrate lineage plasticity at diagnosis and relapse {30209392}.

PAX5 encodes a transcription factor that regulates numerous signalling, adhesion, migration, differentiation, and proliferation genes important for normal B-cell development {17658281; 12479824}. PAX5 mutations are frequently detected in the TCF3::PBX1, BCR::ABL1, and BCR::ABL1-like subtypes {31381561; 19587702} and can be seen rarely in mature B-cell lymphomas {15942942}. Current models propose that PAX5 functions overall as a tumour suppressor gene and that its mutations, including p.P80R, reduce or abolish its normal function, thereby promoting B-cell leukaemogenesis {24013638; 30643249}. The PAX5alt subtype accounts for about 7.5% of B-ALL cases and differs from B-ALL with PAX5 p.P80R in its expression profile, immunophenotype, and prognosis in adults {30643249; 33895809}. Most of the PAX5alt leukaemias have a diverse variety of PAX5 alterations, including rearrangements, point mutations other than p.P80R, and intragenic amplifications {30643249}. More than two dozen translocation partner genes have been reported, all of which create in-frame fusion proteins, with PAX5::ETV6 being the most common. PAX5 p.P80R mutations impair B-lymphoid development, and B-cell leukaemogenesis occurs when a second PAX5 alteration is acquired {24013638; 30643249}. Mutations of the second PAX5 allele, via loss of heterozygosity or an additional PAX5 mutation, are present in nearly all cases {34501239}. Signalling pathway mutations (RAS and JAK/STAT pathway genes, FLT3, BRAF, and PIK3CA) are present in almost all PAX5 p.P80R cases {30643249}.

NUTM1 normally functions as a chromatin modifier by increasing histone acetylation in postmeiotic spermatogenic cells {30257209}. NUTM1 rearrangements occur in as many as one third of infant B-ALL cases that have germline KMT2Avariants, and are associated with a favourable prognosis {33512459}. The majority of the NUTM1 coding sequence fuses in-frame to the 5′ portion of multiple different transcription factor or epigenetic regulator partner genes including ACIN1, AFF1, ATAD5, BRD9, CHD4, CUX1, IKZF1, RUNX1, SLC12A6, and ZNF618 {25730765; 27824051; 30487223; 30643249; 30872366; 33095873; 33512459; 34250504; 34211097}. These fusions result in aberrant NUTM1 overexpression that may potentially alter global chromatin acetylation {30872366; 30487223}, conferring sensitivity to histone deacetylase inhibitors, and possibly to bromodomain inhibitors in NUTM1::BRD9 fusion cases.

MYC encodes a transcription factor that regulates many genes important for proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and immune regulation in many cell types {34372899}. MYC is overexpressed or dysregulated in > 70% of human cancers and is actively studied as a target of precision therapy {31636382; 33397405}. Within B-cell neoplasms, MYC overexpression, because of its translocation to the IGH, IGK, and IGL loci, occurs in Burkitt lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and plasmablastic lymphoma {26980727}. IGH::MYC, IGK::MYC, or IGL::MYC is detected in 0.1% and 4.3% of paediatric and adult B-ALL, respectively {10049049; 33895809}.

There are no unique morphological features.

Immunophenotype
DUX4 rearrangement

Expression of CD371 is seen in almost all cases and CD2 in a major subset {32368831; 30705095}. Monocytic differentiation with expression of CD14, gain of CD45 and CD33, and loss of B-cell antigens is often seen early after induction therapy but may also be present at diagnosis.

ZNF384 rearrangement

Concurrent monocytic differentiation may be seen at diagnosis or early after induction therapy, and the distinction between B-ALL and mixed-phenotype acute leukaemia for this entity is unclear {30209392; 34529760}. It may be reasonable to consider cases where monocytic differentiation is seen on < 5% of the leukaemic cell population as B-ALL until more data emerge. See also section Acute leukaemia of ambiguous lineage with other defined genetic alterations .

These subtypes are defined by their genetic abnormalities as detected by genomic sequencing (DNA or RNA) and/or expression profiling (see the sections on individual subtypes, and #30192Table 4.13). Many cases have additional mutations, but these do not alter the subclassification or diagnosis. Criteria for definitive B-ALL types must not be met, because these frequently have similar mutations {19587702; 33095873}.

DUX4 rearrangement

Next-generation sequencing (RNA and/or DNA) is needed to detect DUX4 rearrangement, mostly with IGH or ERG {27776115; 27019113; 27265895}. Detection of DUX4 rearrangement by conventional cytogenetic approaches is challenging because of the repetitive nature of DUX4 and the insertion of DUX4 into the IGH locus {27776115}.

MEF2D rearrangement

RNA sequencing or RT-PCR is needed to detect the various MEF2D rearrangements, mostly with BCL9 or HNRNPUL1 {27019113; 27824051}. These rearrangements are often cryptic on conventional karyotype analysis {27824051}.

ZNF384 rearrangement

Break-apart FISH or next-generation sequencing (RNA and/or DNA) is necessary to detect the classically cryptic ZNF384 translocations {27392123; 27634205}.

PAX5 p.P80R and PAX5alt

Next-generation sequencing (RNA and/or DNA) is needed to detect the various PAX5 mutations, consisting of sequence mutations, intragenic amplifications, and rearrangement with > 20 different partners {30643249; 33095873}.

B-ALL with PAX5 p.P80R is defined by acquired PAX5 (NM_016734.3) missense mutations that result in a proline-to-arginine replacement at amino acid 80 (p.P80R) within the PAX5 DNA-binding domain (DBD). Detection of PAX5 p.P80R requires DNA sequencing methods. Structural rearrangements of chromosome arm 9p and/or 7p, as well as secondary mutations in signalling pathway genes (#30192Table 4.13), are often observed {30510083; 30643249}. PAX5 p.P80R mutations appear mutually exclusive and are not reported in other B-ALL subtypes {30630978}. Other PAX5 alterations, including gene rearrangements, non-p.P80R sequence mutations, or focal intragenic amplifications, should be classified as B-ALL/LBL with PAX5alt, with the exception of PAX5::JAK2 (Philadelphia [Ph] chromosome–like B-ALL) and PAX5::ZCCHC7, which occurs in cases with other class-defining alterations {30643249}.

NUTM1 rearrangement

Although karyotype analysis can identify a subset of NUTM1 rearrangements with aberrations at 15q14, the exact band is often difficult to discern {25730765; 34211097} and requires break-apart FISH with a NUTM1 probe or RNA and/or DNA sequencing {30872366; 34250504; 34211097}. Of note, NUTM1 break-apart FISH was negative in a SLC12A6::NUTM1 fusion case, probably because of a small inversion limiting signal separation {30872366}.

MYC rearrangement

Karyotype or FISH analysis can detect IGH::MYC, IGK::MYC, or IGL::MYC. Gene expression profiling of this B-ALL/LBL type is distinct from other B-ALL/LBL types {30643249} and from Burkitt lymphoma {30282799}.

Essential: meets the general criteria for B-ALL/LBL (see section B-lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma); demonstration of a specific genetic abnormality as defined in this section; absence of genetic mutations of other B-ALL/LBL types.

Desirable: in B-ALL/LBL with DUX4 rearrangement, increased DUX4 gene expression and/or demonstration of CD371 expression; in adult B-ALL/LBL with MYC rearrangement, exclusion of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma / high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 rearrangements.

As with other B-ALL/LBL types, the prognosis is influenced in part by the genetic mutations (see #30191Table 4.12), but other criteria such as age, white blood cell count, CNS status, early response to therapy, and additional mutations contribute. Of the types listed, DUX4-rearranged B-ALL/LBL has the best outcome, equating to a 5-year event-free survival rate of 95% in children versus 80% in adults {30643249; 33895809; 34250504}, despite a poor measurable residual disease (MRD) response {32646889; 34547766}. The presence of TP53 mutations in this subtype is associated with a poor prognosis {33095873}. MEF2D rearrangement has an intermediate to poor outcome, with a 5-year overall survival rate of about 70% for children and about 30% for adults {27824051; 33895809}. Some cases with DUX4 rearrangement, PAX5 p.P80R, and ZNF384 rearrangement may switch to monocytic lineage during therapy {32646889}. In adults, MYC-rearranged B-ALL/LBL has an inferior outcome, with a 5-year overall survival rate of < 20% for adults {30613837; 33895809}; it has been suggested that Burkitt lymphoma therapy may improve outcome {29112016}. In children, MYC-rearranged B-ALL/LBL is usually treated with Burkitt lymphoma therapy and has a better outcome than the adult counterpart {10049049; 26785246; 29022749}. The prognosis is likely to continue to change as new therapies are introduced and treatments are altered based on minimal/measurable residual disease detection {34529020}.
